hero.headline: No. 9 BYU meets Utah in first top-10 Holy War matchup, drawing national ABC broadcast
hero.body:
No. 9 BYU will face Utah at Rice-Eccles Stadium in the first top-10 clash in the rivalry's history, with millions expected to watch on ABC. The game represents a transformation for what was once a regional grudge match into must-see television for college football fans nationwide.

The rivalry has drawn increasing national attention since Utah joined the Pac-12 in 2011 and BYU went independent with an ESPN deal for its home games. However, Saturday's matchup may represent unprecedented visibility for the in-state showdown, with BYU appearing on a national broadcast network while six other games involving ranked teams compete for viewers.

Greg Wrubell, the voice of BYU Sports Radio Network who has called every rivalry game since 1992, said broad national appeal depends on either or both teams being ranked and in the College Football Playoff conversation. The current matchup delivers both conditions.

What was once described as one of college football's best-kept secrets in Utah has evolved into a game with national playoff implications, marking what observers view as a seminal moment for the Holy War rivalry.

cards.headline: Iran submits nuclear proposal to U.S. as Trump weighs strikes amid divided advisers
cards.teaser: Tehran delivered the proposal through Qatar while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff favor diplomacy and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth supports military action.
cards.body:
Iran submitted a proposal about its nuclear program to the Trump administration through Qatari intermediaries as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Tehran. Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff favor continued diplomacy, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and U.S. Admiral Brad Cooper support renewed military operations, according to The Wall Street Journal.

A senior Iranian official said Tehran demands concrete U.S. action before advancing negotiations, with Ali Bagheri of Iran's Supreme National Security Council saying the country will no longer rely on written commitments from Washington. Trump said Friday that Iran wants to reach an agreement, citing economic troubles and damage to its military capabilities.

cards.headline: Trump replaces chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller after GOP midterm losses
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with longtime adviser Stephen Miller, following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night after Trump blamed her for the election results in which Republicans lost control of Congress. Trump will install Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, in the position starting Monday.

Wiles had offered to resign for two days before Trump accepted her decision Friday. A source who spoke with Wiles said Trump did not directly ask for her resignation but could not stop blaming her rather than himself for the midterm losses. The source said Wiles recognized that if she could not change Trump's view, there was no reason to remain.

Miller, who also served in Trump's first administration, has been working on plans to maintain executive authority despite large Democratic majorities in Congress. A Trump adviser described Miller as a wartime adviser needed to prepare for Democratic investigations. Miller was an architect of Trump's aggressive use of executive power during his first hundred days in office.

Wiles was Trump's longest-serving chief of staff and the first woman to hold the position. She earned an extraordinary level of trust from Trump and often served as the last person he consulted before major decisions. Her influence stemmed from managing his 2016 Florida campaign and his political comeback after the Jan. 6 riot. Wiles had privately opposed the war in Iran and hardline immigration enforcement championed by Miller, policies that contributed to Tuesday's Republican losses.

cards.headline: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
cards.teaser: The vice president has spent two weeks in indirect talks aimed at reaching a ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations.
cards.body:
The vice president has spent two weeks in indirect talks aimed at reaching a ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations.

Vice President J.D. Vance has been speaking almost daily to Qatari and Pakistani mediators about the negotiations, and two weeks ago sent a letter to a senior Iranian official proposing to resume direct negotiations.

cards.headline: China's intelligence agency recruited AI executive to spy on Nvidia CEO, report says
cards.teaser: Alice Huang was enlisted to gather information on Jensen Huang and advanced chip exports, according to The New York Times.
cards.body:
China's Ministry of State Security recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and gather information about American AI chips, The New York Times reported. The intelligence agency allegedly sought to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available to China. Huang has relationships with executives across the AI chip industry, including at Gigabyte.

Three House committees requested that Jensen Huang appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang. President Trump was briefed on the relationship last year but took no action. The two are not related.

cards.headline: Iran-linked tankers loiter over subsea internet cables in Strait of Hormuz
cards.teaser: Vessels with no cargo spent days drifting over cable routes, then switched off tracking systems.
cards.body:
Several tanker ships linked to Iran loitered over subsea internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz in October, according to maritime intelligence firm Windward. The sanctioned tankers, carrying no commercial cargo, slowed down and circled near multiple cables before switching off their automatic identification system transponders. Windward told the Financial Times the behavior suggests the vessels may be mapping cable routes or placing explosives.

Six active cables cross through the Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa, and Asia. Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, depend entirely on the subsea telecommunications connections running through the strait. One third of India's westbound internet traffic passes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Secret Service arrests man near White House with guns who said voices told him to kill Trump
cards.body:
The Secret Service arrested a man Thursday night near the White House after officers found him in a parked vehicle with multiple guns and ammunition and he told them he heard voices in his head telling him to kill President Donald Trump. Officers approached Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos after observing him acting suspiciously in a parked car, according to a Department of Homeland Security statement. Chrinos described hearing voices instructing him to come to Washington and kill the president, the statement said.

Officers subsequently discovered the vehicle had been reported stolen and found three firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition inside. Chrinos has been charged and is in U.S. Marshals Service custody. The department described Chrinos as an immigrant from Venezuela who entered the country illegally through Texas in March 2024.

The arrest is the latest in a series of cases in which the Secret Service and other law enforcement agencies have detained individuals who threatened Trump or members of his family since he returned to office last year. The White House referred questions to the Department of Homeland Security and the Secret Service.

hero.headline: Paraguay's president impeached, arrested after bank collapse left millions unable to access savings
hero.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after lawmakers unanimously voted to remove him from office over the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital bank with links to his private business interests. The bank's demise has left more than half of Paraguay's population—an estimated three million depositors—unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim president and will serve until 2028.

The impeachment passed with 44 of 45 senators voting in favor. Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, had offered to step down Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached him and charged him with misconduct, stripping him of the immunity usually granted to former presidents. Senate President Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of dereliction of duty.

The impeachment charges alleged Peña had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said Peña is due to be questioned Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds. Peña has denied any wrongdoing.

Senator Rafael Filizzola called the situation the biggest corruption scandal in Paraguay's democratic history. In an address to the nation Thursday, Peña said he was sorry and that it was never his intention to betray the trust placed in him. Alliana pledged that citizens affected by the financial collapse would be fully compensated.

cards.headline: Pope Leo XIV begins South American tour in Uruguay weeks after lung surgery
cards.teaser: The pontiff's first stop tests his health as he seeks to reinvigorate Catholicism in a region losing faithful.
cards.body:
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay to begin a South American tour less than a month after undergoing lung surgery. The trip marks his longest journey since the medical procedure and comes as the Catholic Church faces declining membership across Latin America.

During his visit, the pope called for accessible healthcare and urged followers to return to their faith. The tour represents both a test of his physical stamina and an effort to address the church's shrinking influence in a region that remains home to the world's largest concentration of Catholics.

cards.headline: Archaeologists find evidence of cannabis use for psychoactive purposes 2,800 years ago in Siberian tomb
cards.teaser: Seeds and preserved hair from a burial mound suggest drug consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known.
cards.body:
Archaeologists excavating a burial mound in southern Siberia found cannabis seeds and preserved human hair containing active compounds, suggesting psychoactive use of the plant 2,800 years ago, according to a study published in the journal Science. The findings from the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously documented use in neighboring China.

Radiocarbon dating on more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the timeframe. Researchers said the seeds were deliberately deposited within the tomb, indicating the plant had significance in the ancient Scythian community. Some independent experts questioned whether the hair analysis sufficiently distinguished between consumption and external exposure from burial alongside the plant material.

cards.headline: Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE at airport set for release after 24 hours
cards.teaser: Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who has federal work authorization and a pending asylum application, was detained during a targeted operation while boarding a domestic flight.
cards.body:
Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who has federal work authorization and a pending asylum application, was detained during a targeted operation while boarding a domestic flight.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, a 21-year-old Wisconsin state trooper, will be released after being detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Dane County Regional Airport on Thursday while boarding a flight to visit family in New Mexico.

cards.headline: Leonid meteor shower to peak mid-November across U.S.
cards.teaser: The annual Leonid meteor shower will be visible through the end of November, with peak viewing on the night of November 17.
cards.body:
The Leonid meteor shower will be visible across the United States through November 30, with peak viewing expected on the night of November 17. Viewers may see up to 10 to 15 meteors per hour during the peak. The shower consists of dust particles from Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle that enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds up to 44 miles per second, making them the fastest meteors in the sky.

Experts recommend finding a dark location away from light pollution and allowing 20 to 30 minutes for eyes to adjust to darkness. No binoculars or telescope are required. Viewing conditions are expected to be particularly favorable around the mid-November peak because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, reducing light interference.

cards.headline: Justice Department moves to drop lawsuit over California ballots it claimed went to noncitizens
cards.teaser: The federal government sought dismissal after Republicans' midterm losses and days before a hearing on the accuracy of its list of alleged noncitizen voters.
cards.body:
The Justice Department on Friday moved to dismiss its lawsuit seeking to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens. The request comes days after Republican losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was to evaluate the accuracy of the list.

California officials said the list was out of date and included legitimate voters. The motion to dismiss said that by the time of the hearing, the state will have already commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized. The Supreme Court had rejected an emergency appeal to require California to separate the ballots.

cards.headline: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
cards.teaser: A British stuntman is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II after suffering burns and scarring in a 2023 accident during filming.
cards.body:
Edward Sarsfield, a British stuntman, is suing August Street Films after suffering burns covering 15% of his body during a 2023 accident while filming Gladiator II in Morocco. Sarsfield was playing a dead soldier on a burning ship when a gas line used for special effects exploded, causing 20-foot flames that ignited his costume. He was helicoptered to a hospital in Marrakesh and later repatriated to the UK.

Sarsfield is seeking £200,000 in damages and says he has permanent scarring, reduced mobility, and psychological symptoms. August Street Films, a Paramount subsidiary, admits liability for the accident but has not admitted to the alleged injuries or agreed to the damages amount. Paramount said in 2023 that several crew members were hurt in the incident.

cards.headline: Jehovah's Witness died refusing blood transfusion weeks before church reversed 81-year ban
cards.teaser: Isaac Valdez, 26, died in Texas after declining life-saving surgery requiring blood transfusion. Three weeks later, the faith's governing body announced most blood-based medical procedures are now permitted.
cards.body:
Isaac Valdez suffered a brain hemorrhage in August after an epileptic seizure at a Texas library. As a Jehovah's Witness carrying a no-blood card, he refused treatment requiring transfusion. His family honored his wishes, and he died when life support was withdrawn on August 26.

Twenty-three days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body reversed an 81-year prohibition, allowing followers to accept most blood-component medical procedures. The faith's spokesperson described the change as applying scripture to modern medicine but deflected calls for apology. A 2016 medical journal estimated approximately 1,100 Jehovah's Witnesses died annually worldwide having refused blood-based treatment.

hero.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year, Musk says
hero.body:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk said Friday. Musk did not specify whether the company plans to stop making the trucks entirely or shift production elsewhere, but said the decision was to make room for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars. Wes Morrill, the project's lead engineer, wrote on social media that Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab, appearing to suggest the vehicle is being discontinued. Tesla stock rose 4.7 percent Friday after the announcement.

The Cybertruck, known for its angular stainless steel body, was delayed for years before launching in 2023. Sales fell to 20,237 vehicles in 2025 from 38,965 the previous year, according to Kelley Blue Book. Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 after commercial production began in 2023. The vehicle received 146,000 orders when Musk announced it in 2019, though its public introduction was marred when glass Musk claimed was unbreakable shattered during a live demonstration.

The Cybertruck faced several recalls, including one in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 vehicles over concerns that part of the trim could fall off. The vehicle's price also climbed significantly. Musk told analysts the company needed to make it at a price people could afford, which ended up being $61,000 for a fully equipped model. In 2026, the Cyberbeast model costs $102,000.

Musk had called the Cybertruck the best product Tesla has ever made, but questions persisted about whether it could succeed in the competitive U.S. truck market. When a social media user called it the best vehicle Tesla has ever made and lamented its discontinuation, Musk responded with the word true, adding that the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time.

cards.headline: Tesla to end Cybertruck production as automakers shift to smaller electric vehicles
cards.teaser: The massive truck's 123-kilowatt-hour battery will give way to more compact models across the industry.
cards.body:
Tesla will end production of the Cybertruck at its Texas factory next year, part of a broader industry move away from oversized electric trucks with massive batteries. The Cybertruck uses a 123-kilowatt-hour battery weighing around 1,600 pounds, similar to Ford's F-150 Lightning, which was canceled late last year with batteries ranging from 98 to 131 kilowatt-hours.

Automakers are pivoting to smaller electric vehicles with more modest battery packs. Ford plans to launch the Fathom, a sub-$30,000 electric pickup expected to be compact-sized, while Rivian's R2 SUV features an 88-kilowatt-hour battery. Smaller batteries reduce vehicle costs and ease pressure on limited battery supply chains, as the battery pack represents the most expensive component of electric vehicles.

cards.headline: AI stocks recover slightly after multitrillion-dollar market sell-off
cards.teaser: Technology shares rebounded modestly Friday following a rout that began Thursday over concerns about AI regulation and spending.
cards.body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms recovered slightly Friday after a sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off stock values. The Nasdaq Composite closed up 1.1 percent, partially reversing a 5.5 percent drop Thursday, while the S&P 500 rose 0.3 percent. The sell-off was driven in part by investor concerns that a Democratic midterm election victory would bring new AI regulations and questions over whether massive AI infrastructure spending will deliver returns.

Companies including Nvidia, SpaceX, and Tesla regained some ground after losing hundreds of billions in market value. Asian and European markets fared worse, with South Korea's Kospi falling 6 percent and major European indexes declining. Separately, U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above expectations.

hero.headline: Chainalysis says breach exposed credentials and security tokens for all customers
hero.body:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said hackers obtained sensitive information for all of its users, including names, usernames, password hashes, and live security tokens, following a breach of its network. The company's customer list includes government agencies such as the FBI, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the U.S. Air Force, as well as private companies including Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays.

Chainalysis disclosed last Friday that an external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools during an October cyberattack. In an email to affected customers, the company initially said some customer data such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels had been accessed, describing the information as non-sensitive.

In an update Wednesday, Chainalysis said the ongoing multifront cyberattack included an on-path attack that exposed a subset of customer passwords. The company said it had identified and fixed the attack vector. On-path attacks, also known as adversary-in-the-middle attacks, occur when a hacker gains access to infrastructure transmitting traffic between two parties.

Chainalysis has not disclosed where the infrastructure compromise occurred or whether the data obtained was encrypted using TLS. The company has not said whether the data theft exposed customers to additional security threats.

cards.headline: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion in new funding round
cards.teaser: The AI company raised $11 billion but fell short of its original $30 billion target amid a tech stock pullback and shifting public sentiment.
cards.body:
OpenAI reached a $1.25 trillion valuation after raising $11 billion in a new funding round, according to Bloomberg. The company had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation but adjusted its targets after tech stocks declined and midterm election results showed public opinion turning against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI is pursuing additional investments that could bring the total to $20 billion. The company raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation. Chief Executive Sam Altman has said OpenAI is delaying its initial public offering to focus on safety, while rival Anthropic filed to go public last week.

cards.headline: Google takes over unfinished Wyoming data center from Crusoe after cost and timeline concerns
cards.teaser: The search giant is investing $17 billion to develop the site after raising concerns about Crusoe's management of the project.
cards.body:
Google has taken over an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe, a Denver-based developer valued at $30.9 billion, after raising concerns about cost and construction timelines. Google, which Crusoe had tried to land as a customer, announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the campus. The purchase price was not disclosed.

Crusoe originally announced the project last year with plans to scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity. The deal illustrates the difficulty independent developers face delivering massive data center projects on time and within budget, given equipment and power challenges. Despite the setback, Crusoe is building another data center for Google in Texas.

cards.headline: SpaceX strikes deal with Qualcomm to build 5G network for Starlink Mobile carrier ambitions
cards.teaser: The company plans to deploy cellular technology across tens of thousands of cell sites starting in 2027 as it moves to compete with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.
cards.body:
SpaceX has partnered with Qualcomm to build out its planned Starlink Mobile network, bringing Qualcomm's Dragonwing technology to tens of thousands of 5G cell sites across the United States with initial deployments set for 2027. The multi-year deal supports SpaceX's stated goal of making Starlink Mobile a major carrier competing directly with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.

SpaceX has acquired low-band spectrum licenses and is reportedly in talks to access at least 80,000 cell sites through partnerships with tower operators. The company also discussed a potential deal with Boost Mobile that could involve acquiring the budget carrier or accessing its network. SpaceX plans to combine terrestrial cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.

cards.headline: Deep mantle currents may have shaped Great Unconformity, new Nature study finds
cards.teaser: Research suggests slow currents of hot rock pushed continents upward for millions of years, enabling glacial erosion.
cards.body:
Research suggests slow currents of hot rock pushed continents upward for millions of years, enabling glacial erosion.

A new Nature study proposes that slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle helped create the Great Unconformity, a gap in the geologic record spanning between 200 million and more than a billion years. Researchers Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong and Santosh Dhungana argue that mantle currents pushed continents upward for hundreds of millions of years, allowing glaciers to erode them before they sank and were buried by fresh sediments.

cards.headline: Jets' Breece Hall to play Sunday against Chiefs after quad injury
cards.teaser: Running back set to return after five-game absence, will share backfield with Braelon Allen
cards.body:
New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn confirmed that running back Breece Hall will play Sunday against the Kansas City Chiefs after missing five games with a quad injury. Hall's return creates a backfield split with Braelon Allen, who has been productive in Hall's absence.

Glenn declined to detail how carries will be distributed, saying only that "both guys will play." Offensive coordinator Frank Reich called Hall "the bell cow" but indicated the Jets will use a mix of both running backs. Allen ranks third among running backs in rushing success rate this season.

cards.headline: Seahawks rule out seven players including Leonard Williams for Sunday's game against Cardinals
cards.teaser: Seattle will be without its starting quarterback and three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle, among others, as Drew Lock returns to start.
cards.body:
The Seattle Seahawks ruled out seven players for Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals, including three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Leonard Williams (stinger), starting quarterback Sam Darnold (quad, ribs), left tackle Charles Cross (ankle), three-time All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson (knee), edge rusher Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), wide receiver Rashid Shaheed (knee), and backup nose tackle Brandon Pili (back). Reserve edge rusher Connor O'Toole is listed as questionable.

Backup quarterback Drew Lock will start in place of Darnold after being inactive for two games with an elbow injury. Nelson will undergo a minor knee procedure and is week to week after reaggravating an injury. Williams will miss his first game since Week 4 of the 2024 season.

cards.headline: Alcaraz saves two match points to beat Fritz, clinching Jodar's ATP Finals debut
cards.teaser: The Spanish star rallied from the brink in Paris, eliminating Fritz's Turin hopes while securing his compatriot's historic qualification.
cards.body:
Carlos Alcaraz saved two match points to defeat Taylor Fritz 6-7 (10-12), 7-5, 6-3 in the Paris Masters quarterfinals, a result that clinched fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar's qualification for the ATP Finals. Fritz took the first set in a tiebreak and led in the second before Alcaraz rallied, breaking twice to force a deciding set. The 23-year-old dominated the third set to close out the match.

The victory ended Fritz's hopes of reaching the season-ending event in Turin and secured a debut ATP Finals berth for 20-year-old Jodar, who turned professional at the start of 2026. Alcaraz will face either Casper Ruud or Nuno Borges in the semifinals.

cards.headline: WTA chair apologizes to Pegula after private remarks about Andreeva were live-streamed
cards.teaser: Valerie Camillo called the incident "regrettable and unacceptable" after Jessica Pegula's practice-court conversation was broadcast without her knowledge.
cards.body:
Women's Tennis Association chair Valerie Camillo apologized to Jessica Pegula after private remarks Pegula made to her coach about fellow player Mirra Andreeva were inadvertently live-streamed during practice at the WTA Tour Finals on Wednesday. Pegula had called Andreeva a "diva" in what she believed was a private conversation, unaware microphones were recording on practice courts.

Camillo said all audio recording equipment in practice areas has been removed, citing "a failure in our technical execution and monitoring." Pegula, who chairs the WTA players' council, said the incident highlighted ongoing player concerns about privacy as tournaments have expanded surveillance and audio access in recent years.

cards.headline: Brandon Aiyuk's reinstatement talks with 49ers unresolved after meeting
cards.teaser: The receiver met with his agent and the team Friday, but no agreement was reached on roughly $13 million in bonus forfeiture.
cards.body:
Brandon Aiyuk's meeting Friday with agent Drew Rosenhaus and the San Francisco 49ers did not resolve his reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list. Rosenhaus declined to provide further details after the session, saying the parties would issue statements when available.

Aiyuk reportedly owes the 49ers approximately $13 million in bonus forfeiture. The league has delayed his reinstatement while the financial dispute remains unsettled, and the question is whether Aiyuk will agree to a settlement with the team in order to return to the NFL.

cards.headline: Ireland routs Argentina 42-12 with six tries in Nations Championship win
cards.teaser: Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as Ireland dominated Los Pumas in Dublin, but head coach Andy Farrell says his side missed chances to be more ruthless.
cards.body:
Ireland defeated Argentina 42-12 in a Nations Championship match in Dublin on Friday, scoring six tries including a hat-trick from Hugo Keenan. Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast, and Ronan Kelleher also scored for Ireland, which controlled 59% of territory but did not score after the 55th minute.

Despite the 30-point margin, head coach Andy Farrell said the team "missed a chance to be ruthless" with their opportunities. Farrell faces injury concerns ahead of the World Cup in Australia next year, with captain Sheehan failing a head injury assessment and Robert Baloucoune, Josh van der Flier, and Mack Hansen all sustaining knocks.

hero.headline: Godzilla Minus Zero Opens to Record $30 Million-Plus for Live-Action Foreign-Language Film
hero.body:
Godzilla Minus Zero earned an estimated $30 million to $33 million during its opening weekend at the domestic box office, setting a record for the biggest debut ever by a live-action foreign-language film in the United States. The Takashi Yamazaki-directed movie took in $13.5 million on Friday at 3,254 theaters, including $6.7 million from preview screenings. The opening surpasses the previous record held by the 2002 Chinese film Hero, which debuted to $17.8 million.

Distributor Gkids released the film, marking the company's largest opening to date. The movie carried an R rating and received a 96 percent audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Preview screenings for Godzilla Minus Zero began Tuesday and exceeded those of several comparable releases, including Legendary's Godzilla: King of the Monsters, which earned $6.3 million in Thursday previews in 2019 before opening to $47.7 million.

Warner Bros Animation's The Cat in the Hat placed second with a $5 million Friday, including $1 million in previews, heading toward a three-day total between $17 million and $20 million at 4,003 theaters. Angel Studios' Drummer Boy took third place with a $3.8 million Friday and an estimated $9 million opening at 2,850 theaters. A24's You Can See Everything ranked fourth in its fourth weekend with an estimated $8 million to $9 million.

Sony's release of Prime Focus Studios' Ramayana: Rise of the Legend, which opened at 1,433 theaters in the widest North American release for an Indian film, was projected to earn $6 million over three days. In Japan, Godzilla Minus Zero reached 1.38 billion yen, or $8.7 million, through its first three days, with its opening-day gross of 910 million yen setting a record for a live-action film in that market.

cards.headline: 'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Premiere Record
cards.teaser: The Korean fantasy romance drew the highest three-day viewership of any local original launch on the streaming platforms.
cards.body:
Korean fantasy romance "The Remarried Empress" became the most-viewed local original premiere ever on Disney+ and Hulu worldwide, based on its first three days after launching November 3. The series also ranked as the top Korean title premiere in more than 50 markets including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and multiple European and Latin American countries.

Adapted from a popular Naver Webtoon series, the show stars Shin Mina as Empress Navier and Ju Jihoon as Emperor Sovieshu in a story about a marriage and empire unraveling amid political intrigue. The first four episodes are streaming, with new episodes releasing Wednesdays through the November 25 finale.

cards.headline: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult screen-test for next James Bond under Denis Villeneuve
cards.teaser: The actors join a list of contenders for the role after Daniel Craig's departure, with Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight writing.
cards.body:
Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult have screen-tested to play the next James Bond, joining a list of contenders that includes Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, and Jack Lowden. Both British actors bring franchise experience, with Pattinson starring as Batman and Hoult playing Lex Luthor in DC films.

Denis Villeneuve will direct the next Bond film, with Steven Knight writing the script. Amazon MGM Studios, which now oversees the franchise alongside producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, declined to comment on casting. No official announcement has been made.

cards.headline: Adam Driver will not return for HBO's Girls revival
cards.teaser: Driver confirms he will not reprise his role in the limited series set to begin production in 2027.
cards.body:
Adam Driver confirmed he will not return for the upcoming Girls revival, telling Cinema Blend he wishes the production the best of luck. HBO announced in mid-October that the series will return for a limited five-episode run beginning production in 2027, with creator and star Lena Dunham returning as Hannah Horvath alongside original cast members Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells.

Driver's career expanded significantly after his role as Hannah's boyfriend on Girls, including playing Kylo Ren in three Star Wars films and starring in multiple films for directors Noah Baumbach, Ridley Scott, Michael Mann, and Jim Jarmusch.

cards.headline: Melania Trump's Amazon docuseries faces potential House oversight scrutiny
cards.teaser: Incoming Democratic committee leaders signal investigative interest in the first lady's streaming deal as concerns over administration conflicts mount.
cards.body:
Amazon Prime Video is scheduled to release a two-part Melania Trump docuseries on November 20, following the president's party losing control of the House in midterm elections. Representative Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would pursue investigations into what he called administration corruption, telling the Trump family to "lawyer up."

President Donald Trump reported a multimillion-dollar licensing fee for Melania on his 2025 financial disclosure. Amazon spent $40 million to acquire an earlier Melania documentary and $35 million on marketing; the film made about $16.6 million worldwide. The White House has maintained the president and his family have not engaged in conflicts of interest.

cards.headline: Stephen Chow urged Japan to build action films on its own martial arts, says K2 Pictures founder
cards.teaser: Hong Kong director advised Japanese filmmakers to focus on karate and judo instead of imitating kung fu, according to production financier Kii Muneyuki.
cards.body:
Hong Kong star-director Stephen Chow told K2 Pictures founder Kii Muneyuki that Japanese filmmakers should stop imitating kung fu and instead build action films on their own martial arts traditions such as karate, judo, jujitsu and kendo, Kii said Saturday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest. Kii recalled sharing drinks with Chow in Tokyo, where Chow said only Japanese filmmakers can turn those martial arts into action films.

Kii's K2P Film Fund I, which backed director Kore-eda Hirokazu's "Look Back," closed a $33 million equity round in February and is adding loans that will bring the total to $100 million. The fund targets 50 films over seven years. K2 has opened offices in Taiwan and Korea to distribute its films directly in those markets.

cards.headline: Format Executives Detail How 'Suits,' 'Ninja Warrior' Are Adapted for International Markets
cards.teaser: NBCUniversal and TBS officials explain how hit shows are reworked for different countries while preserving core concepts.
cards.body:
NBCUniversal and TBS officials explain how hit shows are reworked for different countries while preserving core concepts.

NBCUniversal and TBS executives outlined how television formats are adapted for international markets at Taiwan Creative Content Fest. Linfield Ng of NBCUniversal Formats cited the Japanese version of "Suits," which replaced marijuana with money in the pilot's briefcase scene because drugs cannot be shown on Japanese television, while Korean and Mongolian versions kept the original drug content.

hero.headline: Trump replaces chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller after GOP midterm losses
hero.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with longtime adviser Stephen Miller, following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night after Trump blamed her for the election results in which Republicans lost control of Congress. Trump will install Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, in the position starting Monday.

Wiles had offered to resign for two days before Trump accepted her decision Friday. A source who spoke with Wiles said Trump did not directly ask for her resignation but could not stop blaming her rather than himself for the midterm losses. The source said Wiles recognized that if she could not change Trump's view, there was no reason to remain.

Miller, who also served in Trump's first administration, has been working on plans to maintain executive authority despite large Democratic majorities in Congress. A Trump adviser described Miller as a wartime adviser needed to prepare for Democratic investigations. Miller was an architect of Trump's aggressive use of executive power during his first hundred days in office.

Wiles was Trump's longest-serving chief of staff and the first woman to hold the position. She earned an extraordinary level of trust from Trump and often served as the last person he consulted before major decisions. Her influence stemmed from managing his 2016 Florida campaign and his political comeback after the Jan. 6 riot. Wiles had privately opposed the war in Iran and hardline immigration enforcement championed by Miller, policies that contributed to Tuesday's Republican losses.

cards.headline: Immigration hardliners celebrate Stephen Miller's promotion to chief of staff
cards.teaser: Deportation advocates see Trump's appointment of longtime immigration hawk as validation their approach has prevailed within the administration.
cards.body:
Immigration hardliners say President Donald Trump's appointment of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff signals their approach to mass deportation has won out within the administration. Miller, who has been one of Trump's closest immigration advisers since 2016, will formally lead the West Wing after months of internal debate over enforcement policy following voter backlash in the midterm elections.

Former Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Mark Morgan and other deportation advocates say Miller's elevation indicates the administration will pursue aggressive enforcement rather than scale back. Mike Howell of the Mass Deportation Coalition called supporters "jubilant" and said he hopes the appointment signals renewed focus on worksite enforcement targeting companies that employ unauthorized immigrants. Miller's new role comes despite Republicans losing ground with Latino voters in Tuesday's midterm elections.

cards.headline: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
cards.teaser: The vice president has spent two weeks in indirect talks aimed at reaching a ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations.
cards.body:
The vice president has spent two weeks in indirect talks aimed at reaching a ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations.

Vice President J.D. Vance has been speaking almost daily to Qatari and Pakistani mediators about the negotiations, and two weeks ago sent a letter to a senior Iranian official proposing to resume direct negotiations.

cards.headline: Sen. Ron Johnson forces GOP meeting to debate midterm losses, pushes to delay leadership vote
cards.teaser: Johnson secured enough signatures to compel a conference discussion on Tuesday's election defeat before scheduled leadership elections.
cards.body:
Sen. Ron Johnson is forcing a Senate Republican conference meeting to discuss midterm election results and delay leadership elections, according to a letter he is sending Monday. Johnson gathered enough signatures under GOP conference rules to require the meeting, which he proposes for Tuesday morning.

In the letter to Conference Chair Tom Cotton, Johnson and supporters called Tuesday's result a "stunning defeat" and argued that holding leadership elections without discussing how candidates intend to lead would be "political malpractice." Senate Majority Leader John Thune remains unopposed to lead the party in the minority next year, and Republicans still expect Tuesday's leadership election to proceed.
